meta.title: Building the Player-Facing Half of a Two-Person Trivia App: Retry Mode, Scoring, and a Shipped Design System
meta.myRole: Frontend developer — game UI/flow, answer scoring, retry mode, points system, and the visual design system. Reviewed and gave feedback on the backend API, but didn't write it myself.

team.name: Fred (CodeByFred)
team.area: Backend — Spring Boot API, database, session tokens, retry/timer logic; some early frontend UI

team.name: Carrie Gale
team.area: Frontend — game flow, answer scoring, retry mode, points system, design system

pitch: A two-person trivia game where players can retry only their genuinely unresolved wrong answers, scored by question difficulty.
problem: Generic trivia apps score a single playthrough and move on — they don't help a player revisit the specific questions they got wrong. This was a 2-person coursework project (frontend: me; backend: my peer) built to add a real retry loop on top of the standard Open Trivia DB question flow: track which answers were wrong, resurface only the still-unresolved ones, and reward harder questions with more points. My side of the work was the entire player-facing experience — the parts a tester actually clicks through — built against an API contract I reviewed in code but didn't write myself.

architectureDecisions.decision: Weighted the points system by question difficulty (easy = 10, medium = 20, hard = 30) instead of a flat per-question score.
architectureDecisions.why: A flat score wouldn't reward attempting harder questions, and difficulty was already a first-class filter on the backend's retry endpoint, so reusing that same field for scoring kept one source of truth for difficulty logic.
architectureDecisions.tradeoff: Score totals are no longer just a raw question count, so any future leaderboard or stats feature has to account for difficulty weighting instead of a simple tally.

architectureDecisions.decision: Built a dedicated Retry Page fed by the backend's filtered game-answers query, instead of reusing the main GamePage component for retries.
architectureDecisions.why: Retry mode needed different behavior — pulling specific past-incorrect answers by archived/wasCorrect status and later marking them archived — which didn't map cleanly onto the main game flow's state.
architectureDecisions.tradeoff: Some duplication exists between GamePage and RetryPage instead of one unified component, since the retry experience was built frontend-first against a backend contract I didn't own.

architectureDecisions.decision: Encapsulated game state, scoring, and save logic in a single GameContext rather than prop-drilling through GamePage's child components.
architectureDecisions.why: Answer scoring, session tokens, and game-over/review data all needed to be readable from multiple UI components (GameOverModal, GameLog, ReviewPage) without threading props through every layer.
architectureDecisions.tradeoff: Most game logic now lives in one context provider, which is convenient for reads but makes isolated testing of individual pieces harder — and the frontend currently has no test scripts defined at all.

architectureDecisions.decision: Time-boxed the right/wrong feedback icon to a fixed 1.5-second window tied to answer submission, instead of navigating to the next question immediately.
architectureDecisions.why: Instant navigation on submit gave no visual confirmation of whether an answer was correct, which feedback on the Figma prototype flagged as confusing during user testing.
architectureDecisions.tradeoff: Every answer submission now has a fixed 1.5s delay before advancing, which slows down play for users who don't need the confirmation, and the planned audio feedback (ding/buzzer) was deferred rather than shipped alongside it.

architectureDecisions.decision: Migrated the live demo deployment from AWS to Render, with the demo database moved from MySQL to Render's free-tier Postgres — the same move made on the employee-creator project.
architectureDecisions.why: The AWS free tier backing the original demo deployment expired, and Render's ongoing free tier covers a small two-person coursework demo without maintaining EC2 infrastructure directly.
architectureDecisions.tradeoff: The live demo now runs on Postgres instead of the MySQL the backend was actually built and tested against (see the repo's `trivia_db_queries.sql` and `application.properties`, both written for MySQL) — as with employee-creator, the live link reflects a cost-driven demo swap, not the documented backend design.

hardestProblem.issue: Retry mode depended entirely on a backend query contract I didn't write myself — `GET /game-answers` requires exact `archived`, `wasCorrect`, and `quantity` parameters plus an optional `difficulty`, and `PATCH /game-answers/{id}` is what actually marks a retried answer as resolved.
hardestProblem.diagnosis: Working mostly from code review rather than the implementation itself, I had to confirm the exact parameter names, types, and required-vs-optional status against my peer's backend before wiring the Retry Page's fetch calls, instead of assuming a shape from the frontend side.
hardestProblem.fix: Matched the Retry Page's queries to the confirmed contract exactly (all three required params, `difficulty` treated as optional), and wired the PATCH call to fire only once a retried question was answered correctly, not just attempted.
hardestProblem.result: Retry mode reliably pulls only genuinely unresolved incorrect answers and stops re-serving ones the player has already corrected.

metrics.label: Delivery cadence
metrics.value: 5 weekly ticket cycles, each shipping a distinct player-facing feature — question display, scoring/context, then retry mode + points + a full design system in the final cycle

metrics.label: Design
metrics.value: Interactive Figma prototype used for real user feedback on visuals and readability before the UI redesign shipped

outcome.limitations: No frontend test scripts are defined yet — the frontend README states this directly — so the trickiest frontend state (scoring, retry archiving) has no automated coverage. The planned audio feedback for right/wrong answers was also never shipped, both logged openly rather than hidden.

whatIdDoDifferently: Nail down the exact backend query contract (archived, wasCorrect, quantity, difficulty) in a shared doc before wiring the Retry Page, instead of confirming parameter shapes through code review after the frontend code was already written.
Add frontend tests before shipping retry mode and the points system — the frontend still has no test scripts, so the trickiest state has no automated coverage.
Ship the planned sound feedback (ding/buzzer) alongside the visual tick/cross icon in the same release instead of deferring it, since half-shipped feedback is easy to forget about later.

Document the AWS-to-Render/Postgres demo migration in the README the same way the original MySQL design is documented — right now the live demo's actual stack isn't mentioned anywhere in the repo's own docs.
